claim: Groupthink as Janis defined it is only partly supported: cohesion alone has no main effect; structural faults (homogeneity, insulation) predict poor decisions better than stress or cohesion; fewer than two dozen empirical tests in 26 years.
agent_test: Do not test the concept; test the remedies below.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Hidden-profile tasks: groups discuss shared information more than unique information and rarely find the best option. Lu et al. (2012) meta-analysis (65 studies, 101 effects, 3,189 groups): hidden-profile groups were about eight times less likely to find the solution than groups with full information. Faulmueller et al. (2010, Experiment 2, figures taken from a researcher note and not re-checked): 1 of 15 hidden-profile groups solved it versus all groups with full information.
agent_test: Split clues across 3 agents so the best answer looks worse to each; measure how often the pooled answer finds it vs one agent given all clues, at equal tokens.
audit_note: The claim glues the Lu et al. 2012 meta-analysis figures (65 studies, 3,189 groups, eight times) onto the Faulmueller sentence; Lu et al. numbers are correct per PubMed, Wikipedia supports the shared-information bias, but the Faulmueller 1-of-15 vs 100% figures could not be checked (paywalled, abstract does not give them).
claim_before_audit: Hidden-profile tasks: groups discuss shared information more than unique information, and rarely find the best option. Meta-analysis (Lu et al. 2012, abstract-level confirmed from a search snippet: 65 studies, 101 effects, 3,189 groups, about eight times less likely; full text not opened). Faulmueller 2010: 1 of 15 hidden-profile groups (7%) vs 100% with full information: 65 studies, 3,189 groups, hidden-profile groups about eight times less likely to find the solution.

claim: Knowing others' preferences before discussion reduces attention to exchanged information and hurts hidden-profile solving (Mojzisch & Schulz-Hardt 2010; abstract-level only).
agent_test: Run agents with and without seeing peer answers before they give independent reasoning; compare.

claim: Human conformity is real: a modern Asch replication (Franzen and Mader 2023, N=202) found a 33% error rate, statistically indistinguishable from Asch's 36.8% (p=.57); a small monetary incentive (1 CHF per correct answer) lowered it to 25%; Bond and Smith's 44 strict replications average about 25%, so rates vary across samples and eras.
agent_test: Baseline: an LLM shown 1-5 confident wrong peers; compare error rate to a no-peer run.
audit_note: The authors call 33% (N=202) a replication of Asch's 36.8% (no significant difference, p=.57), so it is not 'smaller'; only Bond and Smith's 44-replication average (about 25%) is lower, and the paper does not test against it.
claim_before_audit: Human conformity is real but smaller than the iconic 36.8%: a replication gives 33% (N about 202), a monetary incentive lowers it to 25%, and Bond & Smith's 44 replications average about 25%.

claim: A single true dissenter sharply reduces human conformity (Asch variants); minority influence can raise divergent thinking (Nemeth 1986, not re-read).
agent_test: Add one dissenting agent to a majority-wrong panel; measure recovery.

claim: Multi-agent debate beat single agent and majority vote in the original 3-agent, 2-round setting (arithmetic 67.0 to 81.8, GSM8K 77.0 to 85.0, MMLU 63.9 to 71.1, biographies 66.0 to 73.8). Re-checked in the paper.
agent_test: Replicate at equal tokens with a majority-vote-of-N control.

claim: Debate usually does not beat simple baselines even while using more compute: Qwen2.5-7B, average over 7 benchmarks, single 0.7205, majority vote 0.7691, debate T=2 0.7377, T=5 0.7050 (Choi et al.); Zhang et al. found four MAD methods beat CoT in only about 15% of 36 configurations; Smit et al. found no debate protocol reliably better and Medprompt best overall. Under comparable inference budgets on MMLU-Pro, however, Wunderlich et al. report debate (70.0%) slightly ahead of self-consistency (68.7%), so the result depends on how compute is matched.
agent_test: Always compare any panel scheme against a vote of the same number of independent samples.
audit_note: Choi et al. numbers are correct (0.7205/0.7691/0.7377/0.7050), but they and Zhang et al. do not match compute (debate uses more); Smit only says Medprompt performs best/most consistently; and Wunderlich et al. 2026 (in the same note) found debate slightly beat self-consistency at comparable budgets on MMLU-Pro.
claim_before_audit: At matched compute, debate usually does not beat plain majority voting or self-consistency: Qwen2.5-7B average over 7 benchmarks single 0.7205, vote 0.7691, debate T=2 0.7377, T=5 0.7050 (re-checked). Smit et al.: only Medprompt beat the single baseline reliably. Zhang et al.: MAD beat CoT in about 15% of 36 configs.

claim: Debate harm comes largely from correct-to-incorrect flips: LLM agents defer to wrong majorities. Self-correction inside a wrong majority is only 30-34% for strong models and 3.6% for a weak one; inside a correct majority above 97% hold.
agent_test: Measure flip rate of a correct agent shown k wrong peers (k=0,1,2); target low flip rate with unchanged fix rate.
audit_note: The 30-34% / 3.6% / 97% figures are from Knight-Knave-Spy puzzles (where debate overall raised accuracy), and Wynn et al. show C-to-I flips exceed I-to-C but do not quantify 'largely'; the wording is slightly broad.

claim: Mixing a weaker agent into the group can lower accuracy by up to 12 points (MMLU 40.0 to 28.0; 2 plus 1 mix CSQA 58.2 to 50.2). GSM8K improved in the 1+1+1 mix (61.0 to 64.8), so it is task dependent. Verified in the paper table.
agent_test: Vary panel composition by strength at equal tokens.

claim: Heterogeneous model mixes help debate: Heter-SoM +6.4% over SoM average, Heter-EoT +8.2%, up to +5.8% over CoT average (re-checked in table). This conflicts in direction with the Wynn weak-agent harm; setups differ.
agent_test: Compare same-model vs mixed-model panels at equal tokens.

claim: Telling agents to lean toward agreement can raise accuracy (Smit: Multi-Persona +15 points at 90% agreement), while forcing maximal disagreement (0.988) was not best (Liang). Moderate disagreement is best; extremes are bad. New (gap 6): in HiddenBench the best share of instructed dissenters differs by model (GPT-4.1 best at 25%, GPT-5-mini 0% scores 0.000 and peaks at 50-100%, Gemini-2.5-Flash best at 0%), so there is no transferable optimum.
agent_test: Sweep an instructed agreement rate 0-100% on a panel and plot accuracy.
audit_note: Smit reports the gain as 15% (not clearly points) and says disagreement helped on the counter-intuitive dataset, so 'moderate is best' comes mainly from Liang; HiddenBench dissent figures (v4, May 2026) match.

claim: A correctness-payoff instruction in the prompt did not significantly reduce correct-to-incorrect flips (Wynn et al.).
agent_test: Test if payoff or confidence-reporting prompts change flip rate; expect null.

claim: Alignment-trained models are sycophantic: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits a mistake on 98% of are-you-sure challenges; accuracy dropped up to 27% (27% is the are-you-sure drop for Claude 1.3 in the appendix, and the wrong-suggestion drop for LLaMA 2 in the main text).
agent_test: Run an are-you-sure probe on our agent.

claim: Conformity grows with the number of confederates across open models (2 to 10 participants) and a devil's advocate cuts sycophancy (TriviaQA Llama-3-8B base 63.2% to 41.4%; instruct 25.2% to 12.4%).
agent_test: Add a devil's advocate agent; measure flip rate at 1-5 wrong peers.

claim: In Yao et al. (CommonsenseQA, two Qwen agents) adding a centralized judge raised accuracy from 83.62 to 86.65 (single agent 85.50) and lowered the disagreement-collapse rate from 81.71 to 41.27, although DCR is measured differently with a judge and in a three-agent Qwen-Qwen-Llama setup it was higher with a judge (59.09 vs 43.32); judge-free debate showed high collapse. This is suggestive, not a direct test against prompt-based fixes.
agent_test: Compare judge-with-independent-samples vs open debate at equal tokens.
audit_note: Numbers match Yao et al. Table (CSQA, 2 agents), but DCR is defined differently with a judge (judge agrees with a wrong answer), the judged accuracy is only 1.15 points above the single agent (85.50), and in the 3-agent Qwen-Qwen-Llama case DCR is higher with a judge (59.09 vs 43.32); 'works better than prompt fixes' is not directly tested.
claim_before_audit: A structural fix works better than prompt fixes: a centralized judge cuts the disagreement-collapse rate (Qwen-Qwen DCR 81.71 to 41.27) with accuracy 83.62 to 86.65; judge-free protocols leave sycophancy high.

claim: Consensus vs voting depends on task type: voting wins on reasoning (up to 13.2% pooled; MuSR 26.4%), consensus wins on knowledge (up to 2.8% pooled). Approval voting fails to decide in 59% of cases. The two source lines (a28, c08) are consistent (per-dataset vs pooled).
agent_test: Test vote vs consensus rule by task type.

claim: Majority vote success rises with the number of independent agents; belief updates in debate behave as a martingale (no expected gain from discussion alone), so gains come from voting (theory, Choi et al.).
agent_test: Scale N independent samples vs scale rounds at fixed tokens.

claim: Interventions that bias updates toward the majority (Conformist, Follower) raise average accuracy over vanilla debate: Qwen 0.7332 to 0.7625-0.7629 at T=2; oracle 0.8236 (re-checked).
agent_test: Test forced conformity vs independence.

claim: Premature termination and incomplete or incorrect verification are visible failure categories in multi-agent traces, but percent figures were read from garbled text and are unreliable (MAST).
agent_test: Count verification skips in our own traces.

claim: A learned minority-overturn rule helps voting in one lab's test: about one 2:1 split in four (25.5%) has the minority right; a LightGBM classifier on debate-log features gives flip precision 81.2% (39 correct flips, 9 wrong) and net gain +1.71% over six sets, 20 seeds all positive. It is NOT a verifier gate. An LLM judge doing the same job loses 1.37%. No non-author replication found (gap 3 open).
agent_test: Implement minority-overturn with a verifier; measure net gain.

claim: Debate drifts from the task: 170 debates, ten tasks; lack of progress 35% and low-quality feedback 26% as causes.
agent_test: Track topic drift in multi-round runs.

claim: Friendly vs hostile instructions change the strong-agreement share from 70.7-96.3% to 9.5-19.3%, so agreement level is largely a prompt property.
agent_test: Same panel under friendly, neutral, hostile framings; accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: Group polarization is a robust human effect (Walker & Main: judges alone 35% extreme action, three-judge panels 65%).
agent_test: Not directly testable; kept as human context.

claim: People exposed to others' estimates lose diversity and become overconfident (Lorenz et al. 2011; N=144; abstract only).
agent_test: Estimate tasks: compare a panel with and without seeing peer numbers.

claim: Hidden-profile benchmark for LLM panels exists (HiddenBench, 65 tasks, 15 frontier models): panels with split information reach 30.1% vs 80.7% for a single agent with full information. The failure is surfacing information, not reasoning: forced disclosure lifts GPT-4.1 from 0.037 to 0.926. More rounds (peak at 15), bigger groups (gain +0.348 at N=3 to +0.006 at N=7) and tone prompts do not fix it.
agent_test: Split clues over 3 samples/roles so the best answer looks worse to each; test a step that lists unused evidence before committing.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A state-tracking controller that picks challenge / clarify / seek-evidence moves and watches a premature-consensus signal reaches 0.83 average on hidden-profile tasks vs 0.26 for round-robin, and can beat the full-information reference (0.731 average). A structured Exchange-then-Decide protocol also helps across three model families.
agent_test: Add a 'premature consensus' flag to the agent state and test it on a HiddenBench-style task.

claim: Whether discussion beats majority vote depends on whether agents state their private dissent. A mean-field model with four behaviours gives a critical withholding rate; gain falls as withholding rises across 9 LLMs on HiddenBench and MedEInst; value-cohesion instructions push teams into wrong consensus; forcing full withholding nearly removes the gain; turning reasoning off raises gain by lowering internalisation.
agent_test: Record private answer and stated answer separately; never tell the agent to value agreement.

claim: Most measured LLM conformity needs no social source. A bare repeated wrong answer causes harmful revision in 66.5% of initially correct cases (six open instruct models, seven datasets) vs 10.3% for a plain re-ask; an expert-panel frame adds only 12.9 points to 79.4%.
agent_test: Do not show the agent its own earlier wrong sample as a 'peer'; test source-stripped re-asks.

claim: Every tested conformity mitigation trades resistance for receptivity (R-squared 0.80-0.90). Reflection: +7.9 resistance, -15.3 receptivity on MMLU. A unanimous wrong group reverses 22.8% of correct MMLU answers, 54.8% GPQA, 71.0% SimpleQA across 23 open-weight models. Reasoning on self-derivable questions raised both (+7.2, +9.6). Not measured on closed frontier models, so gap 2 is only partly closed.
agent_test: Any dissent operator must be scored on both keeping correct answers and accepting correct corrections.

claim: Decision models over-weight facts held by many agents (social proof) and the full transcript can do worse than no notes: removing attribution tags raises accuracy 13-24 points (small open models).
agent_test: Judge evidence items without counts of how many samples produced them.

claim: At token accounting, a single agent beats structured multi-agent deliberation overall (8.84 vs 8.62; DCI uses about 62x tokens), except on hidden-profile integration where DCI scores 9.56. At comparable budgets on MMLU-Pro debate (70.0%) edges self-consistency (68.7%) and mixture-of-agents is best (71.4%). Dense debating agents have a hard ceiling on effective team size; independent sampling keeps full effective size. No study tests a single agent with an internal dissent step against k-sample voting at equal tokens (gap 1 open).
agent_test: Run this missing test: k samples + vote vs k-1 samples + one critic pass at equal tokens.
audit_note: DCI results are one model (Gemini 2.5 Flash, 45 tasks, no cross-lab check); Wunderlich abstract gives +1.3 and +2.7 while the intro says +1.4 for debate; the 'no study tests... (gap 1)' negative claim cannot be verified from the sources.

claim: Role-played or prompted dissent is only partly reliable for LLMs: it can raise accuracy in some models (GPT-4.1 0.233 to 0.492 with one adversarial agent of four) and lower it in others (Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.889 to 0.306). Human evidence that authentic dissent beats role-played dissent was not re-opened, and no LLM study separates the two (gap 7 open).
agent_test: Compare a self-generated objection with an objection grounded in a check or test, at equal tokens.
